rubric: DISCRETE MATHEMATICS / COUNTING AND LOGIC / CHAPTER 4

slides.title: The binomial theorem, Pascal and the pigeonhole principle
slides.main: Three views of one question — how to count without enumerating.

captions: The binomial theorem, Pascal and the pigeonhole principle
A triangle of numbers, a formula for the power of a sum and a joke about rabbits and cages
In fact these are three views of one question — how to count without enumerating
Today we will see how the pigeonhole principle explains collisions in hash tables

frames.text: two keys in one cell — a collision

body.text: At first glance — a triangle of numbers, a formula and a joke about rabbits and cages. And the pigeonhole principle also explains the collisions in hash tables that you live with every day.

slides.title: Pascal's triangle
slides.main: At the top is a one, along the edges are ones, each number inside is the sum of the two numbers above it.

captions: Let's start with Pascal's triangle: it is built without a single formula — at the top is a one
Along both edges there are ones too
Each number inside equals the sum of the two numbers above it: 1, 2, 1; 1, 3, 3, 1 …
No multiplication, no division — and in the end a table of all the combinatorics of choice

body.text: No multiplication, no division — the triangle honestly grows from a single rule of addition, and in the end you get a table of all the combinatorics of choice.

slides.title: Row n — combinations
slides.sub: Going down from the top is n steps left or right
slides.main: The number in a cell counts the routes to it: and a route is a choice of which of the n steps to turn left on.

captions: Row number n is all the combinations C(n, k), written out in order
Going down from the top, you make n steps left or right: the number in a cell counts the routes to it
A route is a choice of exactly which steps to turn left on: a combination
A grid with obstacles: the number of paths from corner to corner going right and down is the same C(n, k)

frames.text: each cell = left + above, as in the triangle

body.text: A programmer knows a grid with obstacles: the number of paths from corner to corner is the same C(n, k).

slides.title: Properties of rows
slides.sub: The equalities are seen with the eyes, not memorized
slides.main: The triangle is a visual reference book: properties from the chapter on sets are read straight from it.

captions: From the triangle you can instantly read off properties we met in the chapter on sets
The sum of the numbers in row n equals 2ⁿ: a row is all subsets grouped by size
The row is symmetric: C(n, k) = C(n, n − k) — choosing whom to take is the same as choosing whom to leave
Pascal's rule: C(n, k) = C(n−1, k−1) + C(n−1, k) — take a particular element or don't
The triangle is a visual reference book: the equalities are seen, not memorized

body.text: The sum of row n equals 2ⁿ — this is the power set of an n-element set, grouped by the size of the subsets.

slides.title: The binomial theorem
slides.sub: A power of a sum expands along Pascal's row
slides.main: The coefficient of each term is C(n, k): the number of ways to place them in their positions.

captions: Now the binomial theorem: a power of a sum of two terms
In each bracket we take a or b — go through all the ways and add: aa + ab + ba + bb
A term with n − k factors a and k factors b occurs exactly C(n, k) times
The coefficients of the expansion are the whole of Pascal's row: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1

frames.text: ab and ba are one term, so the coefficient is 2

slides.title: Quick estimates
slides.sub: Raise one plus a small number to a large power
slides.main: Expand by the binomial, see the dominant terms and drop the tail — an honest simplification.

captions: The practical strength of the binomial is quick estimates without a calculator
(1 + 0.01)¹⁰⁰ — the main role is played by the term with the small number to the first power
This is how compound interest, load growth under a small daily deterioration and the analysis of algorithms are estimated
The general skill: expand by the binomial, see the dominant terms, drop the tail
Honest simplifications keep the essence and remove the noise

frames.text: sum ≈ 2.70 — the first two terms give 2.00
sum ≈ 2.70 — the first two terms give 2.00
sum ≈ 2.70 — the first two terms give 2.00
the essence stays, the noise goes

body.text: Approximations in the analysis of algorithms are made the same way: the main role is played by the term in which the small number stands to the first power.

slides.title: Inclusion and exclusion
slides.sub: Two sets: from the sum subtract the intersection
slides.main: The cardinality of a union equals the sum of the cardinalities minus the cardinality of the intersection.

captions: We move on to inclusion and exclusion — honest counting over overlapping groups
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|: the common part was counted twice, subtract it once
Forty people started the audio course, thirty watched the webinar, ten did both: 60 reached, not 70
A union in a database returns no duplicates — it quietly does the same for you

frames.text: 2 occurs in both, but in the result — once

body.text: This is exactly what a union in a database does: it does not return duplicates, that is, it quietly performs inclusion and exclusion for you.

slides.title: Three sets
slides.main: The sum of the cardinalities, minus the sums of the pairwise intersections, plus the intersection of all three.

captions: With three sets a pulsation begins: add, subtract, add
The sum of the cardinalities, minus the pairwise intersections, plus the intersection of all three
Out of a hundred people: English — 55, German — 45, French — 25; pairs 18, 12, 8; all three — 5
So eight people know no language at all — without a single enumeration

slides.title: The pigeonhole principle
slides.main: The conclusion is guaranteed by the numbers alone: at least one cage holds at least two rabbits.

captions: The pigeonhole principle is the simplest and the trickiest tool of the course
There are more rabbits than cages: at least one cage holds at least two
However the rabbits are seated — the conclusion is guaranteed by the numbers alone
The principle proves existence but does not say which cage to look in

frames.text: existence is there — the address is not

body.text: The principle proves existence without showing where exactly: we learn that a coincidence exists, but we don't learn which cage to look in.

slides.title: Collisions in a hash table
slides.main: A hash function cannot remove collisions — it can only make them rare and irregular.

captions: For a programmer the principle is a sentence and a consolation at once
A table has four cells, keys can be any number: a collision is not "possible" but guaranteed
From this comes all the machinery: chains in cells, open addressing, growth with rehashing
A hash function does not remove collisions — it only makes them rare and irregular
Fighting the very possibility is pointless; making collisions cheap is sensible

frames.text: collisions remain — but rare and irregular

body.text: Fighting the very possibility of collisions is pointless; designing the table so that collisions are cheap is sensible.

slides.title: Birthdays and hairs
slides.sub: Intuition counts people, but you have to count pairs
slides.main: Classic Dirichlet surprises: coincidences are guaranteed by the numbers, there is no need to look for anyone.

captions: The same principle gives a surprise: in a group of 23 people two share a birthday — more likely than not, although there are 366 days
Intuition counts people, but you have to count candidate pairs: there are almost 250, and each only needs to match
A classic existence proof: in a city of a million, two people have the same number of hairs
There is no need to look for those people — Dirichlet has already said everything

frames.text: two people with the same number of hairs exist

body.text: In a group of twenty-three people it is more likely than not that two share a birthday, although there are three hundred and sixty-six days in a year.

slides.title: Cryptography and finiteness
slides.sub: The same law, only with huge numbers
slides.main: Finiteness is structure, not a detail: the pigeonhole principle will sooner or later remind you of itself.

captions: Even cryptography lives under this law, just with huge numbers
Any hash has a finite space of outputs: with enough files a collision must happen
A good hash function makes the space practically unimaginable — signatures and integrity checks rest on that
Finiteness is structure, not a detail: the pigeonhole principle will sooner or later remind you of itself

frames.text: more files than outputs ⇒ a collision
all the files ever created — a tiny dot on the left
finding a pair is practically unreal
the pigeonhole principle will remind you of itself

body.text: A good hash function makes the space practically unimaginable — digital signatures and integrity checks rest on that.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: The triangle, the binomial, inclusion–exclusion and Dirichlet — counting without enumerating.

captions: Summing up the chapter
Pascal's triangle is a table of combinations built by one addition; rows sum to 2ⁿ
The binomial theorem expands a power of a sum along Pascal's row and gives quick estimates
Inclusion and exclusion fix double counting, and the pigeonhole principle guarantees collisions
Next — propositional logic: we will formally take apart conditions from the if statement

body.text: In the next chapter — propositional logic: we will learn to take apart formally the conditions that you write every day in an if statement.
